v.why: Stepping down from very large learning rates fixes divergence, giving large gains on all three datasets (experiments 12, 14, 18, 19).
Raising an already large learning rate pushes training into instability (experiments 7, 9).
Very small learning rates underfit in 243 epochs, so a larger step helps (experiments 1, 2, 10).
Lowering an already tiny learning rate worsens underfitting, so it helps less than at other learning rates.
Deeper networks are less stable at high learning rates (experiments 47, 50).
Removing a layer stabilizes training when the learning rate is high (experiments 53, 57).
Very strong L2 penalty underfits, so reducing it recovers accuracy (experiments 91, 92, 99).
Increasing an already heavy penalty worsens underfitting (experiments 85, 86).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise, which stabilizes training at high learning rates (experiments 23, 27, 30).
Smaller batches add gradient noise that compounds instability at high learning rates (experiments 34, 38).

raw:
Each hypothesis below rests on the 100 experiments plus a basic sense of how MLP training behaves. The experiments clearly support the learning-rate and alpha-high patterns. The last two (batch size) are weaker. Hypothesis 8 is supported mainly by experiments 23, 27 and 30. For hypothesis 10, experiments 34 and 38 agree but 37 and 40 are mixed, so I would trust it least.
